extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York; citizens, voters, lawyers, and publicmen considering the Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of how the proposed Constitution treats the judicial power and the trial by jury, especially whether civil jury trial is preserved, how federal and state courts share jurisdiction, and which cases are inappropriate for juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of the phrase vesting 'judicial power' in one Supreme Court and such inferior courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause 'The JUDICIAL POWER of the United States SHALL BE VESTED in one Supreme Court, and in SUCH inferior courts as the Congress shall from time to time ordain and establish.' may be construed either to limit federal cognizance to federal courts alone or merely to denote the organs (one Supreme Court and such inferior courts) through which the United States will exercise judicial power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the construction that does not imply an alienation of State power by implication; interpret the phrase as specifying the organs of national judiciary rather than as an exclusive grant that excludes State courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction of State courts in cases arising under federal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts will, by nature of the judiciary power and the system's design as 'one whole,' take cognizance of causes arising under the laws of the Union unless they are expressly prohibited from doing so by future acts of the national legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume State tribunals retain jurisdiction in federal matters where not expressly excluded; view State courts as natural auxiliaries to execute federal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court extends to state court decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution grants appellate jurisdiction to the Supreme Court in enumerated cases without language that confines its operation to appeals from inferior federal courts; the objects of appeal, not the originating tribunal, are contemplated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceive appeals as extending to State tribunals to prevent elusion of national judiciary authority and to ensure uniform national principles of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional discretion to define subordinate federal courts' jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The convention's plan authorizes the national legislature 'to constitute tribunals inferior to the Supreme Court' and does not define whether such subordinate courts shall have original or appellate jurisdiction; these outlines are left to legislative discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize Congress may establish appeals from State courts to subordinate federal tribunals and adjust appellate arrangements to reduce Supreme Court caseload and the need for many federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence in the Constitution does not abolish trial by jury in civil cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution's omission of an express provision for jury trial in civil cases does not imply abolition; silence is distinct from prohibition and cannot be taken to mean civil jury trial is abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply common-sense rules of legal interpretation: an express provision for one thing (criminal jury) does not ipso facto deny the power to allow it in other cases unless clearly incompatible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to constitute courts includes power to prescribe modes of trial
rubrics_metrics.description: A power to constitute courts is a power to prescribe the mode of trial; consequently, absent an express constitutional injunction, the legislature may choose to adopt or omit jury trials for civil causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the legislature as having primary authority to determine mode of trial in civil causes unless the Constitution clearly prescribes otherwise (as it does for criminal jury trials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of jury trial as a safeguard is strongest in criminal cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial by jury is most directly tied to the security of liberty in criminal cases (together with habeas corpus); its constitutional protection there is the chief concern for guarding against arbitrary punishments and prosecutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus constitutional guarantees on criminal jury protections as essential to liberty; civil jury protections are valuable but not necessarily essential in all civil contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury trial as a check against corruption — benefits and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries are a check against corruption because a standing body of magistrates is easier to influence than juries summoned ad hoc, but practical limits exist (sheriffs and clerks select jurors; jurors can be corrupted), so the safeguard is imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the double-security when both jury and bench must be corrupted to pervert justice; nevertheless, do not overstate the absolute protective power of juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability of a uniform constitutional rule for civil jury trial due to state diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is great diversity among States in the extent and modification of jury trials (separate courts of common law, chancery, admiralty, probate, different boundaries between law and equity), making it difficult to draft a single constitutional rule that fits all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imposing one State's system as a federal standard; leaving the matter to legislative regulation and State practice is preferable to a rigid, ill-fitting constitutional provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain causes are unsuitable for trial by jury (prize, admiralty, equity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases concerning the laws and usages of nations (prize causes), admiralty matters, and many equity cases often require legal and policy expertise or long, intricate examination unsuited to lay juries; juries may endanger public policy or foreign rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude or refrain from constitutionally mandating jury trials in such matters; vest determination of these causes in tribunals or procedures appropriate to their technical and public-policy character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of equity from law jurisdiction preserves jury trial's character
rubrics_metrics.description: The separation of equity jurisdiction from ordinary law jurisdiction prevents courts of law from being unduly transformed and avoids subjecting delicate equitable inquiries to jury decision; equity requires prolonged, detailed examination incompatible with jury deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain distinct equity tribunals (or procedures) to protect both the effectiveness of equity relief and the 'pristine purity' of jury trials where they are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections to the Massachusetts formulation limited to actions at common law
rubrics_metrics.description: The Massachusetts proposition ('In civil actions between citizens of different States, every issue of fact, arising in ACTIONS AT COMMON LAW, may be tried by a jury if the parties, or either of them request it.') is confined and vague because what counts as 'actions at common law' varies by State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that such a partial clause either addresses too narrow a class of cases or would operate inconsistently across States until uniform definitions of common-law versus equity jurisdiction are adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineffectiveness of the phrase 'Trial by jury shall be as heretofore' for the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: A provision stating 'Trial by jury shall be as heretofore' would be meaningless for the United States 'as such' because there is at present no antecedent federal judicial system to which 'heretofore' could refer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague referential phrasing that lacks a clear antecedent at the federal level; constitutional language should have operative and unambiguous reference points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem of making federal jury practice depend on the law of the state where the court sits
rubrics_metrics.description: One plausible rule is that federal causes should be tried by jury if, in the State where the federal court sits, that mode would obtain in a similar case — but this creates capricious variability depending on court location and parties' circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about adopting a rule that ties mode of trial to local practice because it may yield inconsistent outcomes for similar federal causes merely due to forum location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over- or under-inclusive constitutional provisions on jury trial
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to draft a constitutional provision on jury trial that is neither too narrow to be useful nor too broad to be advisable; overly precise rules risk impracticality and political resistance, while extreme generality is inoperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor leaving detailed regulation to legislative bodies and the development of practice, recognizing that future experience may justify extensions or abridgements of jury trial in particular cases.
